does not change `b` — so the program prints `cat`.

dog.message: `b = a` copies the value `a` has at that moment. Changing `a` later does not change `b`.

hints: The name is already stored in the variable `name`. How do you print the value of a variable?
`print` can show several values separated by commas: `print("Hello,", name)`.

misconceptions.message: Your program printed the word `name` itself. Remove the quotes around `name` to print what the variable holds.
`+` glues text together without a space. Use a comma, `print("Hello,", name)`, and Python adds the space for you.

steps.text:
A variable can get a new value later in the program. The old value is gone: the variable only
remembers the **latest** value it was given.

lessons.title: Giving a variable a new value

steps.text:
When Python sees a variable's name in your code, it uses the **value** stored in that variable.
Words inside quotes are just text, so `"name"` and `name` mean different things.
